title: Strategic Causal Policy Learning with Manipulable Eligibility
claim: Different fairness and safety objectives are optimized at different decision thresholds, so no single threshold satisfies all of them.
layout: 3 panels in a row, shared x-axis, dashed vertical optimum markers
description: Three side-by-side line plots share the x-axis, the announced threshold k, which runs from about -0.2 to 1.2. Panel (a), in teal, shows strategic welfare as an inverted U. Its peak is marked by a dashed vertical line and a circle at k_max=0.77. Panel (b), in orange-brown, shows worst-group welfare regret as a V shape. It reaches a minimum at k_fair=0.62. Panel (c), in purple, shows harmful treatment falling monotonically to zero. It flattens at k_safe=0.90. Each panel has a bold title, a y-axis label, light gridlines and an italic math annotation giving the optimum. The eye goes first to the colored curves, then to the dashed lines. These sit at three different k values, which shows the tension between the objectives.
caption: Population threshold tradeoffs under the three-group Gaussian design. (a) Strategic welfare $G^S(k)$, (b) worst-group welfare regret $\max_z F_z(k)$, and (c) aggregate harmful-treatment mass $H(k)$. Each vertical line marks the optimum for its corresponding objective (the smallest pointwise-safe threshold in panel (c)).
abstract: The standard rule in unconstrained causal policy learning is simple: treat individuals with nonnegative CATEs. But this rule can fail when treatment eligibility is strategically manipulable. After a policy is announced, individuals may change the covariates used for assignment without changing their underlying treatment effects. We study how such responses affect treatment allocation and welfare. Using an access-burden representation, we characterize strategic treatment and decompose welfare loss into missed beneficial treatment and harmful treatment. For linear CATEs and quadratic manipulation costs, we derive closed-form threshold corrections. When manipulation costs are homogeneous, a single correction recovers the ideal positive-CATE allocation. With heterogeneous costs, welfare maximization, pointwise safety, and minimax group welfare regret can favor different thresholds. Simulations illustrate these tradeoffs and examine the effects of estimating treatment effects and behavioral responses.
